title: Life in God's family
summary: The church is not a building but a family and the body of Christ - a place of community, support, and growth. We explore the meaning of belonging, the unity expressed in obedience to Christ the Head, and the Lord's Supper as a memorial of his sacrifice, with the ordinance of humility. Additional layers: discerning God's will, and the Supper as a memorial in light of the Mass and transubstantiation.

sections.heading: The church is a family, not a building

items.comment: Believers are "members of God's household" - not guests or strangers, but members of the family. The church is first of all people joined together by God, not a place or an institution.

questions.text: What changes when you see the church as a "family" you belong to, rather than a "place" you go to?

items.label: "church" means "a called-out assembly" (ekklesia)
items.content: The Greek *ekklesia* means "the called-out, the assembly" (from *ek-kaleo* - "to call out"), and in the ancient world it referred to a gathering of citizens, not a building. The New Testament never calls a structure a "church" - the church is the people called by God. This is why you can "be" the church, not merely "go" to it.

questions.text: How does your understanding of involvement change when "church" means a community of people rather than a place?

items.comment: "A people who once were not a people" became "the people of God." Belonging to God's family is not something earned - it is a gift that creates a new identity and a community.

questions.text: What does it mean for someone who has felt like an "outsider" to hear that they have been included in "the people of God"?

items.comment: The church is like one body with many members - different, yet mutually needed. No one is unnecessary, and no one is sufficient on their own.

questions.text: Which "members of the body" in your circle of faith tend to be underappreciated - and what does that teach you about yourself?

items.label: "the body of Christ" (soma) as an image of the church
items.content: Paul calls the church *soma Christou* - "the body of Christ." The image says three things: diversity (many different members), interdependence (the eye cannot say to the hand, "I do not need you"), and a shared destiny (when one member suffers, all suffer together). This is not a metaphor for a loose association, but for a living organism in which Christ is the Head and believers are members joined to one another.

items.comment: "The eye cannot say to the hand, I do not need you." When "one member suffers, all suffer together" - community means interdependence and shared feeling, not a loose collection of individuals.

questions.text: When was the last time you experienced someone "suffering with" or "rejoicing with" you in your community?

sections.heading: Unity: Christ as the Head of the body

items.comment: We are to "grow up into him who is the Head - into Christ." The unity of the body does not consist in submission to some earthly authority, but in shared obedience to one Head - Christ. It is from him that "the whole body" draws its growth.

questions.text: What does it mean in practice that Christ - and not some human authority - is the "Head" of the community?

items.label: unity as submission to the Head, not to earthly authority (Eph 4:15-16)
items.content: In Eph 4:15-16 the church's unity and growth flow "from the Head" - Christ, from whom "the whole body" is "joined and held together." The image locates authority in Christ, not in an earthly structure. The unity of Christians is therefore not uniformity under human leadership, but shared submission to one Head and mutual service. Obedience within the community is the fruit of a relationship with Christ, not subjection to an institution - consistent with the principle of sola scriptura.

questions.text: How can you tell the difference between unity "under Christ the Head" and unity forced by human authority?

items.comment: "He is the head of the body, the church." Primacy in the church belongs to Christ - he gives direction and holds the community together.

questions.text: How can you tell whether a community truly "holds to the Head," that is, is guided by Christ?

items.comment: Jesus prays "that they may all be one" - the unity of believers is meant to be a witness to the world. It is not an end in itself, but a sign that the Father sent the Son.

questions.text: In what way can the unity of Christians be "proof" of the truth of the faith to an outside observer?

items.label: unity as witness: "that they may be one" (John 17:21)
items.content: In his high-priestly prayer Jesus asks "that they may all be one... so that the world may believe." The unity of believers is not an end in itself or an organizational uniformity - it is a witness. The model for this unity is the bond of the Father and the Son ("as you, Father, are in me"): unity in love and purpose, while the distinctness of the Persons is preserved. Such unity becomes, for the observer, an argument that God stands behind the church.

items.comment: Unity is "kept" in "humility, gentleness, patience" and by "bearing with one another in love." It is the daily work of relationship, not an automatic state.

questions.text: Which of these attitudes - humility, gentleness, patience - would most help your community?

items.comment: We are "not to neglect meeting together" and to "spur one another on toward love and good deeds." Meeting together is not a formality - it is mutual encouragement, all the more important "as the day" of the Lord's return "draws near."

questions.text: What do you lose when you cut yourself off from the community of believers - and what do you gain when you remain in it?

items.comment: The first Christians devoted themselves "to the apostles' teaching, to fellowship, to the breaking of bread, and to prayer," sharing what they had. This is a picture of a living, practical community, not mere theory.

questions.text: Which element of the early church's life (teaching, fellowship, breaking of bread, prayer) would you most want to see today?

items.label: "fellowship" means sharing and participation (koinonia)
items.content: The Greek *koinonia* (Acts 2:42) means more than "companionship": it is "participation, common ownership, sharing." This is why the first Christians did not merely meet together, but "had everything in common" and shared their goods (Acts 2:44-45). *Koinonia* embraces a community of faith, prayer, the table ("the breaking of bread"), and everyday life. It is the model of a community that is a real sharing of life, not just a weekly gathering.

items.comment: "Carry one another's burdens" - community is a place where burdens are shared, not carried alone. In this way we "fulfill the law of Christ."

questions.text: What "burden" are you carrying alone right now that you could share within your community?

items.comment: God gives the community various gifts and ministries "to equip the saints for the work of ministry" and so that the body may "reach maturity." Spiritual growth happens in community, not in isolation.

questions.text: What gift or ability could you bring to serve others in God's family?

sections.heading: The Lord's Supper: a memorial and the ordinance of humility

items.comment: Jesus institutes the Supper with the words "do this in remembrance of me." The bread and the cup point to his broken body and shed blood - this is a memorial of his sacrifice, not its repetition.

questions.text: What does it mean to take part in the Supper as a "memorial" - what is it meant to keep you from forgetting?

items.label: "memorial" (anamnesis) in Luke 22:19
items.content: The Greek *anamnesis* ("remembrance, recollection") points to a living recalling of a past event, not its renewed accomplishment. "Do this in my *anamnesis*" means: do this in order to remember and to carry in your heart the sacrifice offered "once for all." This is the basis for understanding the Supper as a memorial, not a repeated sacrifice.

items.comment: Before the Supper, Jesus washes the disciples' feet - the task of a slave. This ordinance of humility precedes the Supper and sets its tone: an encounter with a God who serves.

questions.text: What do you feel at the thought of a God who kneels to wash the feet of those who were about to fail him?

items.label: foot washing as an ordinance (John 13:14-15)
items.content: Jesus not only washed the disciples' feet, but plainly commanded: "you also should wash one another's feet... I have set you an example." Many Christian communities practice foot washing as an ordinance of humility preceding the Lord's Supper - a literal carrying out of Jesus' command and a preparation of the heart through reconciliation and service. It is a reminder that we come to the Lord's table in an attitude of humility, not of superiority.

items.comment: "If I have washed your feet... you also should wash one another's feet." Jesus leaves a pattern of mutual, humble service - and promises a blessing to those who follow it.

questions.text: How does the ordinance of foot washing translate into concrete, everyday service toward others?

items.comment: Paul urges us to come to the Supper after "examining ourselves" - in an attitude of sincerity and reconciliation, not "unworthily." This is an invitation to reflection, not to fear.

questions.text: What is worth "examining" in yourself before coming to the Lord's Supper?

items.label: the Supper as a memorial in light of the Mass and transubstantiation
items.content: A sensitive question: in the Supper, do the bread and wine literally become the body and blood of Christ (transubstantiation), and is the rite a renewal of the sacrifice (the Mass)? Scripture presents the Supper as a "memorial" (Luke 22:19 - *anamnesis*) and as "proclaiming the Lord's death until he comes" (1 Cor 11:24-26), not as a repeated sacrifice. The Letter to the Hebrews stresses that Christ's sacrifice was once and sufficient: "once for all" (Heb 10:10), "by a single offering he has perfected for all time" (Heb 10:14). Since it was accomplished "once for all," it does not need repeating. The elements of the Supper remain signs pointing to Christ. The critique concerns the teaching and the rite, never people who in good faith worship God - the measure is Scripture (Isa 8:20).

questions.text: If Christ's sacrifice was "once for all" (Heb 10:10,14), what does that say about what the Supper is and what it is not?

sections.heading: The kingdom of God here and now

items.comment: "The kingdom of God is among you" - it is not only a future reality. The community of God's family is a place where this kingdom is already being realized on earth.

questions.text: Where in the life of God's family can you see that "the kingdom of God is among" people already now?

items.comment: The community is "the salt of the earth" and "the light of the world" - it is meant to influence its surroundings, not to close in on itself. The kingdom is seen when "good deeds" lead people to glorify God.

questions.text: How could your community be more of a "light" for those around it, rather than just a place for "insiders"?

application.text: The church is not a building you go to, but a family you belong to - the body of Christ, in which no one is unnecessary and no one is sufficient on their own. Its unity does not consist in subjection to human authority, but in holding together to one Head - Christ. In community we share burdens, grow, and support one another. The Lord's Supper reminds us of the sacrifice of Jesus offered "once for all," and the ordinance of humility that precedes it teaches us that our God is the one who serves. All of this is, already today, an expression of the kingdom of God among us.
application.challenge: This week, take one concrete step toward community: reach out to someone in God's family, offer help in carrying a "burden," or get involved in one ministry. If you take part in the Lord's Supper, prepare yourself with a moment of sincere reflection and reconciliation (1 Cor 11:28), and treat the ordinance of humility as a pattern for service for the rest of the week.
